papers.title: Redeploying Claude Fable 5
papers.core_contribution: Documents the June 2026 Fable 5 bypass report, Anthropic's comparative severity assessment, and the classifier update used before redeployment.
papers.methodology: First-party incident chronology plus cross-model reproduction and safeguard remediation report; not an independent peer-reviewed study.
papers.key_results: Anthropic reports that the specific technique was blocked in over 99% of cases after the classifier update, and that no universal Fable 5 jailbreak had been discovered at the time of writing.
papers.key_results_location: Timeline and safeguard updates, paragraphs 37-43; safeguard taxonomy, paragraphs 58-64.
papers.limitations: The report is written by the model provider; the underlying Amazon report, prompts, and raw evaluation data are not public in this disclosure.
papers.math_foundations: A qualitative defense-in-depth and severity taxonomy rather than a statistical or formal security model.
papers.motivation: Inference: Anthropic needed to distinguish a narrow safety-margin bypass from unique model-capability release and establish a consistent incident-triage language after an unusually consequential deployment interruption.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: national-security sensitivity and dual-use risk constrained disclosure of the exact method and raw capabilities; the provider also had strong incentives to contextualize severity.
papers.key_decisions: The disclosure compares unlocked capability to widely available models, separates narrow from universal jailbreaks, and reports the mitigation rate instead of publishing an operational recipe.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Not visible; the post says multiple safeguards and a larger safety margin were already used, then a targeted classifier was added.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Comparable public models are a valid counterfactual for capability gain, and provider-run reproduction accurately captures the reported behavior.
papers.relevance_reason: It resolves the user's Fable 5 reference and shows why bypass frequency alone is not the same as security severity.

papers.title: More details on Fable 5's cyber safeguards and our jailbreak framework
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Cyber Jailbreak Severity scale and specifies the intended scope of Fable 5's cybersecurity classifiers.
papers.methodology: Provider-authored normative rubric with four axes: capability gain, breadth, ease of weaponization, and discoverability.
papers.key_results: The proposed CJS scale has five bands, CJS-0 through CJS-4, and four scoring axes; a capability-gain score of zero makes the finding informational regardless of bypass status.
papers.key_results_location: Grading jailbreak severity, lines 102-128; four axes, lines 110-117.
papers.limitations: This is an early draft framework, not a validated benchmark; some axis values require expert and contextual judgment.
papers.math_foundations: Ordinal, banded risk scoring inspired by vulnerability severity assessment, without a validated aggregation model.
papers.motivation: Inference: the incident exposed that the word jailbreak collapses minor policy bypasses and high-uplift capability release into one label.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: the framework must support industry-government communication without publishing sensitive attack details.
papers.key_decisions: It centers marginal capability over existing tools, then separately measures universality, reproduction effort, and discoverability.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Not visible; the text explicitly labels the framework an early draft under partner development.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Experts can compare an unlocked output against existing tools and reliably separate capability gain from weaponization effort.
papers.relevance_reason: It motivates decoupling raw attack success from real-world uplift in any new agent-security harness.

papers.title: A Red-Team Study of Anthropic Fable 5 & Opus 4.8 Models
papers.core_contribution: Measures residual automated jailbreak success on Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 with panel re-adjudication, emphasizing adaptive rather than static attack families.
papers.methodology: Four automated attack families over 7,826 harmful intents; apparent successes re-adjudicated by three judge models using majority vote.
papers.key_results: Worst-case adaptive success is reported as 6.1% for Fable 5 and 11.5% for Opus 4.8; 702 and 1,620 completions respectively were panel-confirmed.
papers.limitations: Single-author white paper; automated intent generation and model-judge adjudication may not measure real-world capability uplift or severity.
papers.math_foundations: Descriptive attack-success proportions with majority-vote adjudication; no causal or deployment-prevalence inference.
papers.motivation: Inference: aggregate refusal rates can conceal a residual surface that sustained adaptive search still finds.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: API-only access forces black-box evaluation and model-panel judging at the reported scale.
papers.key_decisions: Uses a broad intent census, separates attack families, and re-adjudicates apparent successes to reduce judge false positives.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Not visible in the abstract; static obfuscation was retained as a negative comparative family.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The judge panel's majority vote is a valid proxy for harmful completion and the intent corpus represents the relevant surface.
papers.relevance_reason: It is the closest public quantitative study of the model named by the user, but its evidence tier must remain explicit.

papers.title: Best-of-N Jailbreaking
papers.core_contribution: Shows that simple black-box sampling can scale jailbreak success across text, vision, and audio, making test-time attack budget a first-class variable.
papers.methodology: Repeated black-box sampling of non-semantic input variants with automated harmfulness grading across frontier multimodal systems.
papers.key_results: At 10,000 samples the paper reports 89% ASR on GPT-4o and 78% on Claude 3.5 Sonnet; composition with an optimized prefix improves ASR by up to 35%.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract, arXiv lines 22-24; scaling figure and Section 3 in the paper.
papers.limitations: Large query budgets and automated graders can overstate practical accessibility and severity; the work does not measure capability uplift.
papers.math_foundations: Empirical power-law-like scaling of ASR with sample count.
papers.motivation: Inference: robustness claims based on a small fixed query budget are unstable when attack compute scales.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: black-box access motivated a simple scalable method and cross-modal transformations rather than gradient access.
papers.key_decisions: Treats sample count as the independent scaling axis and reports curves rather than one attack budget.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The paper compares modalities and compositions; no discarded search policy is visible from the abstract.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Automated harmfulness grading remains reliable as the number and modality of samples grow.
papers.relevance_reason: It establishes attack-loop budget scaling and the need for budget-matched comparisons.

papers.title: Jailbroken Frontier Models Retain Their Capabilities
papers.core_contribution: Tests whether complex jailbreaks degrade the useful capabilities they unlock and finds the degradation shrinks for stronger models.
papers.methodology: Evaluates 28 jailbreaks on five capability benchmarks across a Claude model capability ladder.
papers.key_results: Haiku 4.5 loses 33.1% average benchmark performance when jailbroken, while Opus 4.6 at maximum thinking effort loses 7.7%; the strongest classifier bypass is reported near-perfect with near-zero degradation.
papers.limitations: Capability benchmarks do not directly measure harmful real-world uplift, and the analysis is limited to the tested model family and jailbreak set.
papers.math_foundations: Descriptive capability ratios across model and jailbreak conditions.
papers.motivation: Inference: safety cases should not rely on a presumed capability tax from elaborate jailbreak wrappers.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: standardized benign benchmarks were used because direct harmful-capability evaluation would be riskier and harder to compare.
papers.key_decisions: Measures post-jailbreak task capability separately from ASR and stratifies by base-model capability.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Performance on the five benign benchmarks tracks the capability retained for security-relevant tasks.
papers.relevance_reason: It separates bypass effectiveness from whether the resulting model remains operationally capable.

papers.title: Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that agent prompt-injection defenses that look strong against static attacks can collapse under defense-aware adaptive evaluation.
papers.methodology: Constructs defense-specific adaptive attacks and evaluates eight indirect-prompt-injection defenses in tool-using agents.
papers.key_results: All eight evaluated defenses are bypassed, with adaptive attack success consistently above 50%.
papers.limitations: Attack adaptation to each defense may not represent attacker knowledge in every deployment; transfer and utility costs require separate evaluation.
papers.math_foundations: Adversarial robustness evaluation under an adaptive threat model.
papers.motivation: Inference: static benchmark success is not evidence of robustness when the defense changes the attacker's optimization problem.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: black-box tool-agent behavior and finite query budgets determine the feasible adaptive search.
papers.key_decisions: Treats the deployed defense as part of the environment and evaluates defense-aware attacks rather than a fixed prompt corpus.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The adaptive attacker has realistic observation and query access to the defended agent.
papers.relevance_reason: It directly supports adaptive harness evaluation and warns against non-adaptive defense claims.

papers.title: FlowSteer: Prompt-Only Workflow Steering Exposes Planning-Time Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.core_contribution: Moves the attack surface from message content to workflow formation by showing that planning signals can reshape downstream multi-agent propagation.
papers.methodology: Black-box and transferred evaluation of prompt-induced workflow steering across planner-executor multi-agent configurations, plus an input-side defense.
papers.key_results: The attack increases malicious success by up to 55% over naive prompting; FlowGuard reduces malicious success by up to 34% while preserving prompt utility.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract, arXiv lines 22-25; full experiments in Section 6.
papers.limitations: The threat model and tested planner-executor settings do not cover all orchestration frameworks; percentage improvements are setting-dependent.
papers.math_foundations: Graph-position and signal-propagation analysis rather than a formal security proof.
papers.motivation: Inference: defenses inspecting only a generated graph are too late if adversarial input already shaped graph formation.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: prompt-only, black-box access was chosen to model an external user without infrastructure control.
papers.key_decisions: Attacks planning-time topology formation, evaluates transfer, and places the defense before graph construction.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Not visible from the abstract; naive prompting is retained as the principal control.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The observed workflow influence transfers beyond the specific planner and benchmark configurations.
papers.relevance_reason: It is direct evidence that graph engineering creates a graph-level security surface.

papers.title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
papers.core_contribution: Defines infinite agentic loops as a framework-dependent systems failure and introduces graph-based static analysis for unbounded costly feedback paths.
papers.methodology: Framework-independent Agent IR and Agentic Loop Dependence Graph analysis over 6,549 public LLM-agent repositories, followed by manual review.
papers.key_results: IAL-Scan reports 74 candidates; manual review confirms 68 failures across 47 projects, yielding 91.9% precision.
papers.limitations: Static detection does not measure exploitability, runtime prevalence, recall, or whether a learned stopping policy preserves task utility.
papers.math_foundations: Dependence-graph reachability to costly or state-growing operations without effective bounds.
papers.motivation: Inference: agent loops are semantic and framework-mediated, so ordinary source-level loop checks miss them.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inferred: large-scale public-repository analysis favors static precision over dynamic coverage and recall estimation.
papers.key_decisions: Builds an intermediate representation across frameworks, detects graph feedback paths, and validates candidates manually.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Public repositories and manually confirmed static paths are representative enough to establish the failure class.
papers.relevance_reason: It is the freshest evidence linking loop engineering, graph structure, denial-of-service risk, and termination.

papers.title: LoopTrap: Termination Poisoning Attacks on LLM Agents
papers.core_contribution: Defines termination poisoning: indirect prompt injection that corrupts an agent's progress judgment and amplifies its execution loop; then profiles and adaptively red-teams that surface.
papers.methodology: A sandboxed simulated-tool study over 10 attack strategies, 8 agents, and 60 GAIA tasks, followed by behavior profiling and adaptive red-team search. This literature review records only the defensive threat model and aggregate evidence, not attack prompts or implementation details.
papers.key_results: Static strategies average 2.33x step amplification; the adaptive framework averages 3.57x with a peak of 25x and 3.93x token amplification. The authors state that comprehensive defenses remain unvalidated and propose independent sandboxed progress verification plus provenance-aware processing.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract and Introduction, arXiv HTML lines 58-92; Discussion lines 352-361; token results lines 443-453.
papers.limitations: Preprint; uses simulated tool returns, a unified ReAct-style harness for main experiments, fixed sampled tasks, and no empirically validated comprehensive defense. Publishing attack templates creates dual-use risk, so this project does not reproduce them.
papers.math_foundations: Step and token amplification ratios plus adaptive-search success under a finite episode budget.
papers.motivation: Progress evaluation is often performed by the same model that consumes untrusted external content, making loop termination a control-flow attack surface.
papers.constraints_inferred: Containment, rate limits, and simulated observations are needed for safe evaluation; the threat requires external content to influence the progress signal.
papers.key_decisions: Targets control flow rather than output content, stratifies task and model susceptibility, and keeps the main execution environment simulated.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The paper does not validate a defense; it explicitly leaves independent progress verification and provenance-aware processing as future work.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Step/token amplification captures relevant denial-of-service risk and simulated observations preserve the termination-poisoning mechanism.
papers.relevance_reason: This is the closest attack to the user's loop-engineering thesis and makes a generic security-aware stopping idea non-novel; the open gap is an adaptive-aware, independently grounded defense.

papers.title: Beyond Attack-Success Rate: Action-Graded Severity Scale for Tool-Using AI Agents
papers.core_contribution: Replaces binary attack success for tool agents with a seven-level trace-grounded action-harm rubric based on reversibility, scope crossing, and privilege expansion.
papers.methodology: Scores AgentDojo tool trajectories using a deterministic oracle and a panel of three language-model judges across four victim models and two defenses.
papers.key_results: Reports that severity grading reveals three cases hidden by binary ASR, including a nominal zero-ASR defense with an externally visible cross-scope leak; judge-panel agreement with the oracle is Krippendorff's alpha 0.91, with escalation-chain blind spots.
papers.limitations: Very recent single-author preprint; ordinal labels depend on rubric validity and attacker-goal context, and the model judges share blind spots.
papers.math_foundations: Ordinal seven-level harm scoring and inter-rater reliability using Krippendorff's alpha.
papers.motivation: Binary compromise labels discard how harmful the executed action actually was.
papers.constraints_inferred: Trace-grounded grading requires complete tool-call records and enough semantic context to judge reversibility, scope, and privilege.
papers.key_decisions: Uses an independently specified deterministic oracle beside model judges and reports their systematic disagreement.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Binary ASR alone is rejected as an adequate severity instrument.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The seven levels preserve a meaningful order of real-world harm and logged actions capture the consequential behavior.
papers.relevance_reason: It crowds a generic beyond-ASR severity project and forces any Fable-inspired evaluation direction to measure marginal capability or orchestration effects beyond this action-graded rubric.
